description: Somos un equipo entusiasmado por aprender y dar nuestro apoyo en el estame espacial, contamos con las habilidades de software que puedan involucrar este desafío, si alguien quiese unirse este es el espacio ideal porque somos un equipo que busca integrar distintas disciplinas e ideales
summary:
Planet X Explorer is an educational web platform that guides students and curious members of the public through the process of comparing infrared images of the sky. We developed a tool in which users select a region and two observation dates, then view both images alongside a difference map that highlights preliminary signals. Users can adjust the detection threshold and export the results. The tool has two modes: a synthetic Demo for safe practice, and an on-demand connection to SPHEREx observations through NASA/IPAC IRSA.

The challenge is that astronomical archives are open to everyone, yet their data are hard to interpret without technical training. Our project addresses this by turning a specialized workflow into a clear, step-by-step experience, with built-in lessons and a visible label showing whether each image is simulated or real. It uses the search for the hypothetical Planet Nine only as a starting point, and it never claims a detection.

This matters because it teaches a core scientific habit: a bright difference between two images is not a discovery until it has been checked against noise, instrumental effects, and independent evidence. In this way, the project promotes scientific literacy and critical thinking, in line with quality education.
details:
What it does and how it works. Planet X Explorer turns a technical astronomy workflow into a guided, step-by-step experience. Users enter sky coordinates and a cutout radius, or pick a suggested region. They search for available epochs, choose a compatible pair, and receive image A, image B, and a residual map (B − A). For real data, the system requires the same collection and detector, different dates, and at least 80% spectral overlap. It then reprojects image B onto A, removes the background, and computes the difference. Preliminary signals are highlighted using a robust noise estimate, and users can adjust the threshold between 2σ and 10σ, select signals, and export a CSV with provenance. The platform also includes three lessons and a five-question quiz.

Benefits. The project makes scientific literacy more accessible by teaching how to handle uncertainty, evidence, and critical review. It is reproducible, its code is public, and it needs no permanent server, so it can run at zero hosting cost.

Intended impact. We plan to use it in classrooms, technology fairs, and outreach activities in Cajamarca, so that participants learn to distinguish simulation from observation, interpret an image subtraction, and explain why a signal needs further verification. This impact is expected, not yet measured. It supports SDG 4 and, secondarily, SDG 9.

Tools and technologies. The backend uses Python 3.12 and FastAPI, with NumPy, SciPy, and Astropy for processing, and HTTPX, SIA2, and optional Gaia DR3 queries for external services. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We tested with pytest, Playwright/Edge, and axe, managed versions with Git and GitHub, and used OpenCode with Sol 6.1, Astra, and DeepSeek for AI-assisted development. The only hardware was a general-purpose Windows computer; no sensors or GPU were needed.

Creativity. Our contribution is one of integration and education, not a new detection technique. We combine visible provenance, interactive comparison, and built-in explanations in a single tool. Progress bars reflect confirmed milestones rather than fake loading animations.

Factors we considered. We kept simulated and real data strictly separate, with no silent fallback when a request fails. We labeled all results as preliminary, since a 5σ signal does not prove a planet exists. We also designed for mobile devices, keyboard navigation, and reduced motion, and we documented the scientific limits openly.
